enrichment.short_title: NASS duties for disabled children of asylum seekers

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970

key_facts: A Turkish asylum seeker and her severely disabled sons lived in unsuitable temporary accommodation arranged by Hackney and subsidised by NASS.
NASS and Waltham Forest failed to find wheelchair-accessible replacement housing near the boys' special school despite repeated requests.

The claimants argued NASS breached section 122(3) and that Waltham Forest was barred only from duplicating NASS support, not from providing better accommodation under section 17 or section 2 of the Local Government Act 2000.
Keith J held current accommodation was 'adequate' within section 122(3) by applying the Westminster/Ouji demarcation between central and local support for disabled dependants.
He ordered Waltham Forest to reconsider increased direct payments under section 17A for disability-related expenditure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of NASS and Waltham Forest refusal to provide suitable accommodation and adequate financial support.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review claim dismissed save for an order requiring Waltham Forest to decide whether to make increased section 17A payments.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 122(3) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, 'adequate accommodation' for a disabled child of a destitute asylum seeker means accommodation that would be adequate if the child were not disabled; where NASS is complying with that limited duty, section 122(5) prevents a local authority from providing alternative accommodation under section 17 of the Children Act 1989.
legal_issues: Whether unsuitable stairs-only housing is 'adequate accommodation' under section 122(3)
Whether section 122(5) disapplies local authority duties under section 17 and section 2 of the Local Government Act 2000
Whether Article 8 requires a broader reading of NASS accommodation duties
Whether Waltham Forest breached section 100(2) by failing to assist NASS in finding suitable housing

enrichment.short_title: Costs after repudiatory breach contract appeal
key_facts: Following the main appeal in Bim Kemi AB v Blackburn Chemicals Ltd, Blackburn were held the overall successful party on liability.
Blackburn sought full indemnity costs relying on late disclosure and a 29 May 2001 'drop hands' settlement offer.
Bim argued for no trial costs and only 50% of appeal costs because Blackburn lost on the 'no contract' issue.
The court ordered Bim to pay 75% of Blackburn's trial and appeal costs on the standard basis.
Interest on costs was awarded at 1% over base rate for pre-judgment costs and at the judgment rate from 30 January 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal costs judgment following adjourned costs issues after substantive contract appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Blackburn awarded 75% of trial and appeal costs on the standard basis; various interest and assessment orders made; costs of Blackburn's own loss assessment deferred.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a successful defendant ran and lost a major issue, proportionate reduction of costs is appropriate; a reasonable pre-trial settlement offer may negate criticism of litigation conduct but does not entitle the offeror to ignore issue-based costs consequences or to indemnity costs.
legal_issues: Who was the successful party for costs purposes
Whether Blackburn's loss on the 'no contract' issue should reduce costs
Whether indemnity costs were warranted
Appropriate rate of interest on costs
Whether costs of assessing Blackburn's own damages should be payable now

key_facts: Mrs Erekin obtained Southwark housing by fraudulent application and was imprisoned for related frauds.
Her five children had lived stably in the four-bedroom property since 1997.
The county court judge refused a possession order as unreasonable in all the circumstances.
Southwark appealed, arguing the judge failed to weigh severe housing shortage and the scale of the fraud.
Laddie J dismissed the appeal, holding the judge's balancing exercise was within the permissible discretionary range.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a county court refusal to grant a local authority possession order.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal from a discretionary possession decision, the appellate court may intervene only if the judge exceeded the generous ambit within which reasonable disagreement is possible; omission of every argued factor from an extempore judgment does not show the factor was ignored.
legal_issues: Whether the judge failed to take housing shortage into account
Whether the scale of fraud required a possession order
Correct test for interfering with a county court discretion

enrichment.short_title: Humber Bridge large bus toll statutory construction
key_facts: The Confederation challenged tolls levied on large buses crossing the Humber Bridge under 1997, 2000 and 2002 Tolls Revision Orders.
The 1997 and 2000 orders defined 'large bus' but omitted it from the operative toll schedule; explanatory notes and decision letters showed an drafting mistake.
The 2002 order omitted 'large bus' entirely; the judge treated large buses as goods vehicles by axle count.
The Court of Appeal held the 1997 and 2000 orders could be read to include 'large bus' in class 4 under Inco Europe principles.
For the 2002 order the court preferred reading in a class 4 £10 maximum for all large buses rather than the judge's axle-based goods-vehicle approach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from refusal of judicial review of Humber Bridge Board toll decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Board held authorised to charge large buses up to £9.20 (1997), £9.60 (2000) and £10.00 (2002).
enrichment.ratio: Where a tolls order plainly contains an inadvertent omission, the court may read words into delegated legislation if the intended purpose, drafting mistake and corrective wording are abundantly clear; extrinsic materials such as decision letters and inspector reports may be used when the instrument is ambiguous or absurd.
legal_issues: Whether large buses were within the 1997 and 2000 Tolls Revision Orders
Whether courts may correct obvious drafting errors in statutory instruments
Whether large buses fell within 'goods vehicle' in the 2002 order
What extrinsic materials are admissible in construing toll orders

enrichment.short_title: Deferred Shoelanco share purchase price summary judgment
key_facts: Finsoft agreed to sell its Shoelanco shares to Rowil for a minimum US$10 million under July 1993 and September 1993 closing documents.
Finsoft received US$7.5 million but Rowil refused the final US$2.5 million tranche, arguing revised triggers in the variation letter never occurred.
Events meant neither the put nor call option would be exercised and Rowil retained worthless Shoelanco shares after Super Channel was sold.
Tomlinson J held the parties never intended Finsoft to bear the risk that the final tranche might never become payable.
Summary judgment was granted for US$2.5 million with payment due from 1 July 1998.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Part 24 summary judgment application on unpaid deferred consideration under share sale agreements.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for Finsoft for US$2.5 million against Rowil and guarantor CLBN; payment due since 1 July 1998.
enrichment.ratio: Where commercial parties contract for a fixed minimum price but a subsequent variation replaces a certain long-stop date with conditional triggers, the court will construe or imply terms so payment cannot be avoided by events neither side contemplated, especially where the payor's own conduct made the triggers impossible.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 6(iv)(c) of the September 1993 variation letter
Whether Finsoft took the risk that payment triggers might never occur
Whether an implied term, estoppel, rectification or Sudbrook v Eggleton machinery applied
Scope of the put and call options in the Shareholders' Agreement

enrichment.short_title: Proprietary estoppel defeated by unclean hands
key_facts: Orange Contract Scaffolding agreed heads of terms with the Gonthiers for a five-year lease with a £50,000 purchase option and entered possession.
OCS's solicitors marked correspondence 'subject to contract'; the Gonthiers later refused to include the purchase option in the lease.
OCS spent money improving the yard believing it would acquire the property; the recorder awarded £19,500 on proprietary estoppel.
At trial OCS's expenditure claims were found exaggerated and supported by fabricated or misleading documents; VAT-evasion cash payments were admitted.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal on clean hands alone and set aside the estoppel award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from county court possession and proprietary estoppel counterclaim judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; estoppel award and charge set aside; counterclaim dismissed; rent arrears order preserved.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant seeking equitable proprietary estoppel must come with clean hands; serious document fabrication and deliberate inflation of expenditure can bar relief entirely, and negotiations marked 'subject to contract' generally prevent reliance on pre-contract expenditure unless exceptional unconscionability is shown.
legal_issues: Whether OCS had clean hands for equitable relief
Effect of 'subject to contract' on proprietary estoppel
Requirements for proprietary estoppel between prospective landlord and tenant
Whether Gonthiers' assurances were sufficiently clear and irrevocable

key_facts: Synthon sought revocation of SmithKline Beecham's paroxetine methanesulfonate (mesylate) patent for lack of novelty over Synthon's earlier unpublished application.
The judge held the earlier application anticipated the patent by a broad 'same invention' approach aimed at preventing double patenting.
Example 1 of the earlier application did not enable crystalline mesylate matching claim 1; repetition experiments failed until conditions were materially altered.
The Court of Appeal held novelty requires clear enabling disclosure or inevitable result, not equivalence at the same level of generality.
The appeal was allowed and the revocation claim dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against first-instance revocation of UK patent GB 2336364.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; patent held valid for lack of anticipation.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(3) anticipation is governed by ordinary novelty principles, not a special double-patenting test comparing inventions in substance; a prior application must contain clear and unmistakable directions whose performance makes the claimed invention available, and adapting a failed example with hindsight does not anticipate.
legal_issues: Correct approach to novelty under section 2(3)
Whether the earlier application enabled crystalline paroxetine mesylate of claim 1
Whether example 1 produced the claimed polymorph inevitably
Admissibility of general teaching when a specific example fails

key_facts: Chief Moshood Abiola died in 1998 leaving competing 1989 and alleged forged 1994 wills.
Independent administrators were appointed under the 1989 will after prolonged probate disputes involving Princess Zainab Abiola.
About £666,538 from DHCL share sales was held subject to an undertaking because of the will challenge.
Administrators sought court authority to pay professional fees and fund urgent Summit Oil licence work preserving estate assets.
Collins J authorised receipt of DHCL funds and estate-preservation payments without appointing new administrators.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court directions application in pending probate validity proceedings concerning the estate of Chief Abiola.
enrichment.outcome: Administrators authorised to give good receipt for DHCL monies and make payments properly incurred for the benefit of the estate; beneficiary distribution application not granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a common-form grant of administration remains valid pending probate proceedings, the court may authorise administrators to collect encumbered assets and pay fees necessary to preserve the estate, provided payments would benefit the estate whichever will is ultimately upheld.
legal_issues: Whether administrators' appointment should be ratified or replaced
Authority to use DHCL funds held under undertaking
Payment of solicitors', accountants' and oil-licence advisers' fees pending trial
Whether interim distributions to beneficiaries were appropriate

key_facts: BASF challenged SmithKline Beecham's paroxetine hydrochloride anhydrate patent GB 2297550.
The judge held 'substantially free of bound propan-2-ol' in claim 3 meant free of propan-2-ol even when acetone was the production solvent, invalidating several claims.
SB appealed on construction; BASF cross-appealed contending process claims 10(i) and 11 were anticipated by earlier application 407.
The Court of Appeal rejected SB's synecdoche construction and upheld invalidity of claim 3; claims 10(i) and 11 survived.
Experiments showed example 1 of 407 produced hemihydrate, not the claimed displacement process product.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal and cross-appeal from Patents Court validity decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on construction; cross-appeal dismissed; claims 10(i) and 11 held valid.
enrichment.ratio: 'Substantially free of bound propan-2-ol' bears its ordinary meaning and is not a synecdoche for whichever solvent was used; prior art must contain clear enabling directions or inevitable result, and material deviations from a failed example to reach the claimed product do not destroy novelty but prevent anticipation.
legal_issues: Construction of 'substantially free of bound propan-2-ol'
Whether claim 3 was anticipated where acetone, not propan-2-ol, was used
Anticipation of displacement process claims by application 407 example 1
Obviousness of the displacement process
